The human genome contains approximately 3.2 billion base pairs (bp) organized across 23 chromosome pairs. Protein-coding genes number roughly 20,000-25,000 (fewer than initially predicted by the Human Genome Project, or HGP). Gene expression is regulated at multiple levels: (1) transcriptional (promoter methylation, histone modification), (2) post-transcriptional (alternative splicing, mRNA stability via miRNAs), (3) translational (ribosome binding efficiency, codon usage bias), and (4) post-translational (phosphorylation, ubiquitination, glycosylation). Non-coding regions (previously dismissed as "junk DNA") comprise approximately 98% of the genome and include regulatory elements (enhancers, silencers, insulators), structural sequences (centromeres, telomeres), and transposable elements (constituting roughly 45% of total genomic content). Next-generation sequencing (NGS) technologies have reduced whole-genome sequencing costs from $2.7B (the original HGP) to under $200 per genome. Clinical applications include pharmacogenomics (tailoring drug selection based on CYP450 enzyme variants), carrier screening, and tumor profiling for precision oncology.
